planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring into lean, well-drained soil; avoid rich or heavily amended beds, which encourage floppy growth.

directions: Carousel was selected for a notably sturdy, upright clump that resists splaying open under snow load or heavy rain, a common flaw in wild-type little bluestem. New spring growth emerges blue-green streaked with pink, gradually shifting through the season to a fall palette of copper, beige, and mahogany that persists well into winter. It performs best in lean, dry to average, well-drained soil in full sun and struggles in rich or consistently wet ground. Shear the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new shoots appear.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring; give it plenty of room since it grows tall and holds a large upright clump by late summer.

directions: Indian Warrior is a patented big bluestem selection whose blue-green summer foliage shifts early to deep bronze and purple, intensifying to near-burgundy by fall well ahead of the species. It tolerates a wide range of soils from clay to sand, thrives in average to dry conditions once established, and needs no staking despite its height. Site it toward the back of a border or in a mass planting where its dark color and turkey-foot seed heads read as a strong vertical accent; cut the clump to a few inches in late winter.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean to average, well-drained soil; this selection was bred for high-plains conditions and resents heavy, waterlogged ground.

directions: Windwalker was selected through the Plant Select program for powdery, silvery-blue foliage that stands out against typical green-leaved big bluestem, turning deep plum-purple as burgundy seed plumes rise above the clump in late summer. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once rooted in, reflecting its high-plains breeding, and holds an upright, sturdy habit without flopping. Use it as a bold textural and color accent in a dry meadow planting or xeric border, and cut the clump back hard in late winter before new growth starts.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps tolerate considerable drought.

directions: Indian Steel is a long-standing indiangrass selection prized for foliage that reads more consistently silvery-blue than the variable wild species, holding that cool color through summer before the plant sends up bronze-gold flower plumes on tall stems in early fall. It forms an upright clump that pairs well with warm-toned prairie companions like little bluestem and rudbeckia, and needs no staking or division for many years. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil; its narrow, upright profile makes it a good fit for tighter spacing than typical indiangrass.

directions: Thin Man was selected from a wild population near the New Mexico-Texas border for a distinctly narrow, columnar habit that holds itself upright without splaying, unlike the broader-spreading wild species. Blue-green foliage rises tightly through summer and is topped by golden plumes in early fall, offering vertical structure with a much smaller footprint than a typical indiangrass clump. It is very drought tolerant once established and works well repeated in a row or tucked into a narrow bed. Cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; give it room to spread its tall, arching flower plumes without crowding neighbors.

directions: Pink Flamingos is a hybrid muhly grass, a cross between Lindheimer's muhly and pink muhly, combining the taller stature and evergreen-in-mild-winter foliage of the former parent with the vivid rose-pink autumn plumes of the latter. Slender gray-green leaves form a narrow, fountain-like clump topped from fall into early winter by tall arching sprays of pink bloom that read almost as a haze from a distance. It is markedly drought tolerant once established and holds up well in coastal and southern gardens; comb out old foliage or cut back hard in late winter in colder parts of its range.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into lean, fast-draining soil; it excels in rocky, sandy, or otherwise poor ground and resents heavy wet clay.

directions: Honeycomb is a patented blue grama selection bred by Brent Horvath for a tidy, refined clump of fine gray-green foliage and outsized ornamental appeal from its seed heads. In mid to late summer it sends up slender stems carrying golden, comb-like or eyelash-shaped seed heads that hold their form and color well into winter, giving the plant its name. It thrives in poor, lean, well-drained soils and tolerates extended drought once rooted in, making it a fitting choice for a xeric bed, rock garden, or short-grass prairie planting. Trim back old growth in late winter before new shoots emerge.
